question: What is the waiting period for pre-existing diseases?
gold_answer: 36 months of continuous coverage. A rider can reduce it to 24 or 12 months if bought at inception or first renewal.
context:
[1] (source: pre-existing-conditions)
[Waiting Periods and Pre-Existing Diseases]
A waiting period is a stretch of continuous coverage that must elapse before a
particular kind of claim becomes payable. Waiting periods run from the date of
first policy commencement, not from each renewal, provided coverage has been
continuous without a break of more than 30 days.

[2] (source: exclusions)
[Permanent Exclusions > Two things people expect to be excluded but are not]
  pre-existing disease rules if diagnosed before the policy start.

[3] (source: pre-existing-conditions)
[Waiting Periods and Pre-Existing Diseases > What counts as pre-existing]
Hypertension, diabetes mellitus, and cardiac conditions declared at proposal
stage are treated as pre-existing and carry the 36-month waiting period unless
Aurora explicitly waives it in writing on the policy schedule.

[4] (source: pre-existing-conditions)
[Waiting Periods and Pre-Existing Diseases > Schedule of waiting periods]
| Category | Waiting period | Applies to |
|---|---|---|
| Initial waiting period | 30 days | Any illness other than accident |
| Accidental injury | Nil | From day one |
| Specified illnesses and procedures | 24 months | See list below |

[5] (source: senior-citizen-plan)
[Aurora Senior Care — Plan for Ages 60 and Above > Waiting periods]
| Category | Waiting period |
|---|---|
| Initial | 30 days |
| Specified illnesses | 24 months |
| Pre-existing disease | **24 months** (shorter than the 36 months on retail plans) |
answer: For retail plans, pre-existing diseases carry a 36-month waiting period unless explicitly waived in writing [3][5]. Under the Aurora Senior Care plan for ages 60 and above, the waiting period for pre-existing diseases is reduced to 24 months [5]. Waiting periods run continuously from the date of first policy commencement provided coverage does not lapse for more than 30 days [1].

question: How long is the grace period for an annual policy?
gold_answer: 30 days for annual policies (15 days for instalment policies). Cover does not operate during the grace period; it only preserves continuity of waiting periods and no-claim bonus.
context:
[1] (source: policy-renewal-and-portability)
[Renewal, Grace Period, and Portability > Grace period]
The grace period is **30 days** from the renewal due date for annual policies
and **15 days** for policies paid in instalments.

[2] (source: policy-renewal-and-portability)
[Renewal, Grace Period, and Portability > Grace period]
Renew after the grace period expires and the policy is treated as fresh. All
waiting periods restart, accumulated no-claim bonus is lost, and fresh
underwriting applies.

[3] (source: policy-renewal-and-portability)
[Renewal, Grace Period, and Portability > Grace period]
Cover is **not** in force during the grace period. A claim for an admission that
occurs inside the grace period, before the renewal premium is received, is not
payable. What the grace period preserves is *continuity*: renew inside it and
your waiting periods and no-claim bonus carry forward unbroken.

[4] (source: premium-and-payments)
[Premium, Payment, and Tax > Payment modes]
Annual, half-yearly, quarterly, and monthly. Instalment options carry a loading:
half-yearly 2%, quarterly 3%, monthly 5% over the annual premium. Instalment
policies have a 15-day grace period rather than 30.

[5] (source: life-insurance-grace-and-revival)
[Aurora Life — Grace Period, Lapse and Revival > Grace period]
| Premium mode | Grace period |
|---|---|
| Annual, half-yearly, quarterly | 30 days |
| Monthly | 15 days |

Unlike health insurance, **life cover continues during the grace period**. If
the life assured dies within the grace period, the claim is paid less the
outstanding premium.
answer: The grace period for an annual policy is 30 days from the renewal due date [1][5].

question: What is the free-look period?
gold_answer: 15 days from receipt of the policy document, or 30 days if sold through distance marketing.
context:
[1] (source: life-insurance-grace-and-revival)
[Aurora Life — Grace Period, Lapse and Revival > Free-look]
15 days from receipt, or 30 days for policies sold through distance marketing.

[2] (source: policy-renewal-and-portability)
[Renewal, Grace Period, and Portability > Free-look period]
A new policyholder may cancel within **15 days** of receiving the policy
document (**30 days** if the policy was sold through distance marketing) and
receive a refund of premium less proportionate risk premium for the period of
cover, medical examination costs, and stamp duty.

[3] (source: glossary)
[Glossary]
**Free-look period** — The window in which a new policy can be returned for a
refund.

**Grace period** — The window after the due date in which a renewal premium may
be paid without losing continuity. Cover does not operate during it.

**Indemnity** — Reimbursement of actual expenses incurred, up to a limit, as
opposed to a fixed payout on the occurrence of an event.

[4] (source: regulatory-disclosures)
[Regulatory Disclosures > Free-look and cancellation rights]
Statutory rights under the applicable regulations, reproduced in
`policy-renewal-and-portability`.

[5] (source: premium-and-payments)
[Premium, Payment, and Tax > Refunds on cancellation]
Cancellation by the insured after the free-look period attracts a short-period
scale: 75% refunded if cancelled within 1 month, 50% within 3 months, 25% within
6 months, and nil thereafter. No refund is payable if a claim has been made in
the policy year.
answer: The free-look period is the window in which a new policy can be returned for a refund [3]. It lasts for 15 days from the receipt of the policy document, or 30 days if the policy was sold through distance marketing [1][2]. During this timeframe, a policyholder who cancels receives a premium refund minus the proportionate risk premium for the cover period, medical examination costs, and stamp duty [2].

  not supported by prevailing Indian medical practice.
- Rest cure, respite care, custodial care, and convalescence at any facility.
answer: A day-care procedure is a medical procedure that requires less than 24 hours of hospitalisation due to technological advances, making it payable despite the general 24-hour admission requirement [3]. Out-patient treatment is not considered a day-care procedure [3].

question: Does Aurora use a TPA?
gold_answer: No. Aurora administers its own claims and does not use a Third Party Administrator.
context:

[Glossary]
**Sum insured (SI)** — The maximum Aurora will pay in a policy year, before any
no-claim bonus or restoration.

**Third Party Administrator (TPA)** — An intermediary that processes claims on
an insurer's behalf. Aurora administers its own claims and does not use a TPA.

**UIN** — Unique Identification Number allotted to an insurance product by the
regulator.

[2] (source: regulatory-disclosures)
[Regulatory Disclosures > Solvency]
Aurora maintains a solvency ratio above the regulatory minimum of 1.50. The
ratio as at the last audited quarter is published in the Public Disclosures
section of the corporate website, updated quarterly.

[Aurora App — User Guide]
How to use the app. Policy terms are not in this document.

There are two routes. Which one is available depends on whether the hospital is
in the Aurora network, not on the plan you hold.

For employer-sponsored group policies with 50 or more lives. **Individual and

answer: No, Aurora administers its own claims and does not use a TPA [1].

question: What is the minimum number of beds a facility needs to count as a hospital?
gold_answer: At least 10 in-patient beds in towns with a population below 10 lakh, and at least 15 elsewhere.
context:

[Network Hospitals and Cashless Access > Minimum hospital definition]
For a facility to qualify as a hospital under the policy it must have at least
10 in-patient beds in towns with a population below 10 lakh, or 15 in-patient
beds elsewhere; a qualified nursing staff present around the clock; a fully
equipped operation theatre where surgical procedures are performed; and daily

[2] (source: network-hospitals)
[Network Hospitals and Cashless Access > Minimum hospital definition]
patient records accessible to Aurora's authorised personnel.

[3] (source: hospital-cash-benefit)
[Aurora Hospital Cash Benefit > Conditions]
- A minimum continuous hospitalisation of **48 hours** is required. A 30-hour
  admission pays nothing, even where the indemnity claim is payable.
- The first day of each admission is a deductible day and is not paid.
- Maximum 15 consecutive days for any single admission on Options A and B.

[4] (source: plan-bronze)
[Aurora Bronze — Plan Terms > Day-care procedures]
150 listed day-care procedures are covered. Procedures outside the list require
a minimum 24-hour admission to qualify.

[5] (source: network-hospitals)
[Network Hospitals and Cashless Access]
Aurora's network covers 11,400 hospitals across 780 towns as of 1 April 2026.
The authoritative list is the hospital locator in the Aurora app and on the

answer: To qualify as a hospital under the policy, a facility must have at least 10 in-patient beds in towns with a population below 10 lakh, or at least 15 in-patient beds elsewhere [1].

question: I am on Silver with a 5 lakh sum insured and took a room at Rs 15,000 per day. Will everything be paid?
gold_answer: No. The Silver room-rent limit is 2% of 5,00,000 = Rs 10,000/day, so an eligibility ratio of 0.667 is applied by proportionate deduction to all room-linked charges (room, surgeon, anaesthetist, nursing, OT, investigations). Pharmacy and consumables are not reduced.
context:
[1] (source: claims-process)
[Filing a Claim > Worked example — proportionate deduction]
An insured on Silver with a ₹5,00,000 sum insured has a room-rent limit of
2%, i.e. ₹10,000 per day. They occupy a room at ₹15,000 per day for 4 days.
The eligibility ratio is 10,000 ÷ 15,000 = 0.667.

[2] (source: plan-silver)
[Aurora Silver — Plan Terms > Sub-limits]
| Item | Silver limit |
|---|---|
| Room rent | 2% of sum insured per day |
| ICU charges | 4% of sum insured per day |
| Cataract surgery | ₹40,000 per eye |
| Knee or hip replacement | ₹2,50,000 per joint |
| Modern treatment (robotic surgery, oral chemotherapy, stem cell therapy) | 50% of sum insured |
| Ambulance | ₹5,000 per hospitalisation |

[3] (source: plan-bronze)
[Aurora Bronze — Plan Terms > Sub-limits]
On a ₹3,00,000 sum insured the room-rent limit is ₹3,000 per day, which is
below the single-private-room tariff at most metropolitan tertiary hospitals.
Proportionate deduction will therefore apply to most Bronze claims in those
hospitals. Buyers should read the worked example in `claims-process` before
choosing Bronze.

[4] (source: plan-silver)
[Aurora Silver — Plan Terms > Sum insured and premium band]
Silver is available at sum insured of ₹5,00,000 or ₹10,00,000, on an individual
or family-floater basis. Family floater covers self, spouse, and up to three
dependent children under 25.

[5] (source: claims-process)
[Filing a Claim > Worked example — proportionate deduction]
| Head | Billed | Payable |
|---|---|---|
| Room rent (4 days) | ₹60,000 | ₹40,000 |
| Surgeon and anaesthetist | ₹1,20,000 | ₹80,000 |
| Nursing and OT | ₹45,000 | ₹30,000 |
| Investigations | ₹30,000 | ₹20,000 |
| Pharmacy and consumables | ₹25,000 | ₹25,000 |
| **Total** | **₹2,80,000** | **₹1,95,000** |
answer: No, everything will not be paid [1][5]. Under the Silver plan with a ₹5,00,000 sum insured, the room-rent limit is 2% (₹10,000 per day) [1][2]. Because the room cost of ₹15,000 per day exceeds this limit, proportionate deduction applies based on an eligibility ratio of 0.667, meaning only a reduced proportion of applicable billed charges will be payable [1][5].

question: My mother is 63 and I want to add her to my policy. Which plans allow it and what changes?
gold_answer: Dependent parents can be added on Silver (at extra premium), Gold and Platinum, but not on Bronze. Premium is set by the eldest member's age, and on Silver a 10% co-payment applies to every claim once the eldest insured is above 60. Aurora must present a separate senior-citizen policy as an alternative in writing.

| Dependent children under 25 | Up to 2 | Up to 3 | Up to 4 | Up to 4 |

| Dependent parents-in-law | No | No | Yes | Yes |

[3] (source: dependents-and-family-floater)
[Dependents and the Family Floater > Adding and removing members]
  rest of the policy year at no change in premium. If the deceased was the

Premium is determined by the age of the **eldest** member covered. Adding a

On some plans. See `dependents-and-family-floater`.

**What if I miss my renewal date?**
There is a grace period. Cover does not run during it. See
`policy-renewal-and-portability`.

**Is dental covered?**
Not in the base plan. There is an optional rider.
answer: Dependent parents can be added to the Silver plan (at an extra premium), Gold plan, and Platinum plan, but cannot be added to the Bronze plan [1]. When adding a parent, the policy premium is determined by the age of the eldest member covered, which often costs more than an individual senior-citizen policy for that parent [4].
